title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as Savings
dek: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued for repayment and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take, you should still take.
why: Three people in different situations (a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner) each run their own numbers, turning the new rules' 20 clause changes into concrete decisions. The second half on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the system-inside track is especially informative.
who: Employees who have a provident fund but aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a provident fund loan, or contributing on their own as flexible-employment workers; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chit-chat about how the episode came about and where the three hosts stand can be fast-forwarded; start from 13:10, where Zhou Yi's experience of using it.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi set up Beijing's provident fund no-threshold rental withdrawal of 2000 yuan a month, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran dry at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai points out this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can and use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian reminds them that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine for themselves — people just keep fake books for themselves.

points.h: The provident fund is not savings; not being able to take it out is the norm
points.body: Yubai walks through an extreme scenario: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the provident fund, but the home is self-occupied, so it qualifies neither as a home purchase nor as renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the name of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, there is nothing to be done. If you risk it and invent a pretext for fraudulent withdrawal, you will be pursued to return the entire withdrawn amount and barred from any provident fund withdrawal for three years. So both ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate above demand deposits’ hold up; the key is the individual situation.

points.h: The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating a self-occupied home and paying property fees on a self-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the provident fund no longer serves only the single purpose of a loan to buy a home. Second, rental withdrawal used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal scope. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management centre should reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

points.h: The share of provident fund contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: The figure Lao Qian saw: of this year's provident fund contributions, the share lent out is as low as just over 30%, while at the peak it was over 70% — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. This directly reflects how low the willingness to buy a home is. Lao Qian also points out that the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can be withdrawn, thresholds cut sharply — supporting measures as the property market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the ageing trend: the monthly rise in the withdrawal ratio began in 2023, exactly matching the retirement of the 1960s cohort.

points.h: If you want to buy a home, be careful about withdrawing your provident fund
points.body: Yubai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance; in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has several caps, and at application the smallest of the standards applies — for example, a minimum 20% down payment for a first or second self-occupied home means a 1 million yuan home cannot be financed beyond 800,000 yuan; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before taking the provident fund out as living expenses, check your city's loan rules first. Yubai is also cautious about the buying logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio close to the provident fund rate, only a down payment short’: you also have to consider depreciation of the home, rises and falls in prices, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 yuan down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: For flexible-employment workers the contribution base and rate are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The contribution base must be self-declared: below 10,000 yuan no proof is needed; above 10,000 yuan you must log into the individual income tax app and check your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 yuan at 10% to 24% is 1000 to 2400 yuan, and this money is not counted toward individual income tax, but it is a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow one-off back payments.

points.h: Inside the system, the provident fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend back home with a public-institution post, who readily showed a screenshot of her provident fund account: the monthly credit is more than twice Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeds her savings; the friend lives at home with no rental need, so the provident fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus she has an occupational annuity, and the contribution base counts bonuses and allowances in full. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, and with the individual pension capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, being inside the system already carries an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the average annual wage of urban non-private unit employees nationwide was 129,441 yuan, versus 71,590 yuan for private units — while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full provident fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a more desirable choice’ has not changed at all: a company that pays the provident fund in full shows it respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run in every respect, and won't play cat-and-mouse with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximisation the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, you actually take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130, and everyone along the chain feels wronged. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T pay raise — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it was not because the capitalist had a conscience, but because the utility function worked out better that way.

quotes.text: It arrived, but because your phone gets so many app notifications you don't look carefully — say it tells you 2000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is used up and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people just keep fake books for themselves; people withdraw on the spur of the moment for all sorts of reasons; people are very good at deceiving themselves.
You really can't treat the provident fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can take out at any time, but the provident fund you can't.

And it's the highest-quality lending channel, the rate is so low, yet only a bit over 30% of people actually took a loan — and at the peak before, what was that share? Over 70% — in just a few short years.
I think a company that pays the provident fund in full shows it respects its employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean raising costs; it also means one person's spending, the household sector's spending, becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages — the two form a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you can and use everything you can — buying a home, building a home, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country — all of it can be used.
